analysis.title: Global Economics Comment: A Moderate Boost to DM Inflation from AI Demand
key_insights: Central bankers at the Fed, ECB, BoE, RBA, Riksbank, SNB and others increasingly cite the AI buildout as an inflation driver. Their comments focus on supply bottlenecks, higher import prices, and a timing mismatch between near-term domestic demand pressure and later, more uncertain productivity gains.

GS refreshes its global model to size AI-related inflation in developed markets (DMs). It extends the US team's recent US analysis. Three channels directly lift inflation: memory prices in consumer baskets, spillover of memory costs into consumer electronics, and higher electricity prices from data center power demand.

Direct pressure is currently limited in most economies, at around 0.1pp. Memory cards carry tiny basket weights, so the effect is only 2-3bp on year-over-year core inflation in most countries. US PCE is the exception: GS says the software and accessories weight overstates the effect, which adds 23bp (GS forecast for September).

The biggest change from GS's last update is that higher memory prices are starting to spill into phones, computers and video game consoles. These categories carry much larger weights in global baskets. They currently add less than 0.1pp to year-over-year core inflation across DMs, with the largest effects in Japan and US PCE.

GS's US team estimates that consumer electronics spillovers will ultimately raise US core PCE by 13bp in 2027Q1. Rescaled by basket weight, digital equipment price increases add about 10bp on average to DM core inflation, or 18bp relative to long-run trends. The largest uplifts are in US PCE and Japan.

Data center power demand raises US core PCE by 0.1-0.2pp. The effect is under 5bp this year elsewhere because data center ramp-ups outside the US are smaller. GS expects a somewhat larger power price boost in Australia in 2027 and beyond as capacity additions accelerate.

Combined direct pressure currently adds 44bp to US core PCE (GS forecast for September), of which 20bp is mismeasurement of software and accessories inflation. US core CPI, which does not have that mismeasurement, is boosted by 13bp. GS expects peaks of 50bp for core PCE in 2026Q4 and 19bp for core CPI in 2027Q1.
Outside the US, GS expects a peak uplift of about 25bp on core CPI on average in 2027Q1. It comes mostly from consumer electronics price increases that should mostly appear in the next few months.

Indirect pressure through higher activity is small. GS puts the DM GDP uplift at 0.3% through end-2026 and 0.5% cumulative by end-2027. Australia sees the largest effect, the UK and Euro Area the smallest. Production of data center inputs is concentrated in Asian exporters, and passthrough from output gaps to inflation is muted, so the inflation boost from this channel is under 0.1pp.

Overall, GS sees a moderate 0.2-0.3pp boost to non-US DM core inflation through 2027Q1, with the US at about 0.6pp for core PCE and Japan at 0.3pp. GS says this supports some of the policymakers' concerns. It expects the impulse to fade sharply on a sequential basis in most DMs in 2027H2 as AI electronics input price pressure diminishes.
GS relies on its equity strategists' view that memory prices are near their peak, so it expects only modest further upside to memory-exposed categories.

risk_factors: Supply bottlenecks in chips, specialized labor and energy-intensive data center buildout raise prices (Schnabel, SNB's Tschudin).
Higher import prices, such as computer equipment pushed up by AI demand (BoE's Pill).
Timing mismatch: AI demand pressure arrives before uncertain, lagged productivity gains (RBA's Bullock, ECB).
Memory prices could stay elevated longer than GS's equity strategists' view that they are near a peak, which would extend the electronics price boost.
Larger-than-expected power price increases in Australia in 2027 and beyond as data center capacity additions accelerate.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI-related price pressure gives developed-market core inflation a meaningful but temporary boost through 2027Q1 that fades in 2027H2 as memory price pressure diminishes.
theme_stances.evidence: suggesting some of the AI-related inflation concerns expressed by global policymakers are warranted
